If this was a better instrumented region, an event like this would also be useful for trying to understand the significance of low to zero aftershock productivity for deep earthquakes (catalog completeness magnitude is probably too high to say much about aftershocks to this event).

The trade off is that they tend to be much less common than shallower earthquakes, and many approaches can compensate for poorer quality data with simply having more of it to average observations out (this is the same idea as "fold" in active source studies to improve signal-to-noise ratios).
Deep, moderate to large magnitude earthquakes are also pretty good targets for directivity studies, and I think (but am not sure) this may be true for other source analysis approaches.

Moderate to large deep earthquakes are optimal for teleseismic receiver function sources and some types of teleseismic tomography because their sources tend to be significantly less complex than shallow earthquakes. (But shallow earthquakes still tend to be pretty usable).
If there are stations directly above a deep focus earthquake, it might allow higher frequency (so finer vertical spatial resolution) receiver functions than possible with teleseismic earthquakes.

So, to make an entirely unsatisfactory answer, sort of!

Local/regional tomography is going to be iffy--you need crossing raypaths for an earthquake to be useful.

This means an event won't give us much info on stuff directly above it.
